lesson.title: Where the Action Happens: Introducing Critical Points
lesson.summary: A critical point is any point in a function's domain where the derivative is either zero or does not exist, the complete list of places a local extremum could possibly be hiding, though landing on the list is no guarantee of actually being one.
lesson.body:
A number c is a critical point of f, or the input to a critical point, if c is in the domain of f, and either f'(c) = 0 or f'(c) does not exist. This definition deliberately covers two very different looking situations under one name, because both situations share the same consequence: something unusual happens to the slope of the graph right at c, either it flattens out completely, or it fails to be well defined at all, perhaps because of a sharp corner in the graph.

Here is why this definition earns its importance. Suppose f has a local maximum or local minimum at some interior point c, and suppose f is differentiable there. The reasoning from the last two sections showed that the tangent line must be horizontal at such a point, since the function cannot switch from rising to falling, or from falling to rising, without passing through a moment of zero slope. So f'(c) = 0 is forced. Now suppose instead f is not differentiable at c, perhaps the graph has a sharp corner there, like the graph of the absolute value function at x = 0. The function can still turn around at a corner, going down into the corner and back up out of it, without ever having a single well defined tangent slope at that instant. Either way, whether the derivative is forced to zero or fails to exist, the input value c must be a critical point. Put together, this means every local maximum and every local minimum, wherever the function is defined and continuous there, must occur at a critical point. Critical points are therefore the complete list of candidates worth checking, nothing that is not a critical point can be a local extremum.

See this connection directly using the running example. For f(x) = x^3 - 3x, the derivative is f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3, defined for every real number, so the only way to get a critical point here is f'(x) = 0. Solving gives x^2 = 1, so x = -1 or x = 1, both inside the domain. These are exactly the critical points at x = -1 and x = 1, and they are exactly the same two locations where the previous two sections found a local maximum, height 2, and a local minimum, height -2. The theory and the earlier hands on calculation agree.

Now for the crucial warning: being a critical point does not guarantee being a local extremum. It only means the point survives to the candidate list, it still has to be checked. The classic example is f(x) = x^3. Its derivative is f'(x) = 3x^2, and f'(0) = 0, so x = 0 is a critical point. But look at what actually happens near x = 0: for x slightly negative, say x = -0.1, f(-0.1) = -0.001, which is less than f(0) = 0. For x slightly positive, say x = 0.1, f(0.1) = 0.001, which is greater than f(0) = 0. The function is smaller just to the left of 0 and larger just to the right of 0, meaning f is simply increasing straight through x = 0, momentarily flattening its tangent but never turning around. There is no peak and no valley there at all, just a brief pause on the way up. So x = 0 is a critical point of x^3 that is not a local extremum, proof that a critical point is only ever a candidate, never an automatic conclusion. The next several sections build out the vocabulary for talking about these candidates precisely, and eventually a reliable test for sorting out which ones are genuine extrema and which ones, like this one, are not.
